blocks.text: Say you have a spreadsheet of a thousand sales numbers and someone asks you for the total, or the biggest single sale, or which row that biggest sale actually came from. You are not looking for every single number anymore, you are looking for one honest summary pulled out of the pile. That squeezing of many numbers down into fewer numbers is exactly what aggregation functions do in NumPy, and they are some of the most used tools you will ever reach for once you start working with real data.

blocks.caption: This is the whole idea of aggregation in one picture: numbers go in, a summary comes out.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441971928-286996748.png
1. Introduction

This lesson covers the reduction side of NumPy: np.sum, np.min, and np.max as the core reducers, the axis parameter that controls which direction they collapse, np.argmin and np.argmax which hand back a position instead of a value, the cumulative functions np.cumsum and np.cumprod, and the keepdims parameter that controls whether a squeezed dimension disappears entirely or sticks around as a placeholder of size 1.

One thing this lesson deliberately skips over is mean, median, and standard deviation. Those are aggregation functions too, technically, but they get their own full treatment in the Statistical Operations lesson, since they come with their own set of rules around variance and spread. Here the focus stays narrow: sums, extremes, positions, and running totals.

blocks.title: Why this matters for ML/AI work
blocks.content: You will use np.sum to total up a loss across a batch, np.max and np.min to check the range of your data, and np.argmax constantly to turn raw classifier scores into an actual predicted label. These are not academic exercises, they show up in nearly every training loop and evaluation script you will ever write.

blocks.text: 2. np.sum, np.min, np.max: The Core Reducers

These three functions are the simplest possible aggregations, and once you understand how they behave, the rest of this lesson is really just variations on the same theme. np.sum adds every number in an array together. np.min finds the smallest number. np.max finds the largest number. Each one takes a whole array and hands back a single value when you do not tell it anything else.

code.content:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([72, 88, 95, 60, 81])

print(np.sum(scores))   # 396, every score added together
print(np.min(scores))   # 60, the lowest score
print(np.max(scores))   # 95, the highest score

blocks.alt: np.sum, np.min, np.max: The Core Reducers
blocks.caption: With no axis specified, the whole array collapses into one number.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972240-292619407.png

Notice that scores itself is a 1-dimensional array with shape (5,), and every single one of these calls returns a plain scalar, shape (). That is the defining trait of a reduction: dimensions go in, and fewer dimensions come out. Sum, min, and max are also available as array methods directly, so scores.sum(), scores.min(), and scores.max() do exactly the same thing as the function calls above.
2.1 What Reduction Actually Means

It helps to think of these functions as collapsing a dimension rather than just returning an answer. A 1-D array has one dimension to collapse, so with no axis argument it collapses all the way down to a single scalar. A 2-D array has two dimensions, so it can collapse in more than one way, and that is exactly what the axis parameter controls, covered in the next section.

items: np.sum adds every value together and returns their total.
np.min returns the smallest single value found anywhere in the array.
np.max returns the largest single value found anywhere in the array.
With no axis given, all three collapse an array of any shape down to one plain scalar.

blocks.text: 3. The axis Parameter

Real data is rarely a flat list. It is usually a 2-D table, rows and columns, and a sum over the whole table often is not what you want. You might want one total per column, or one total per row, and that is precisely what the axis parameter lets you choose.

Picture axis=0 as pointing down through the rows, and axis=1 as pointing across through the columns. Summing along axis=0 collapses the rows together and leaves you with one value per column. Summing along axis=1 collapses the columns together and leaves you with one value per row.

code.content:
print(M.sum(axis=0))   # [5 7 9], one total per column, shape (3,)
print(M.sum(axis=1))   # [ 6 15], one total per row, shape (2,)

blocks.caption: axis is 0 means walk down through the rows, collapsing them into a single row of column totals.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972242-160725971.png

blocks.caption: axis is 1 means walk across through the columns of each row, collapsing them into one total per row.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972243-259027258.png

blocks.title: The direction is the opposite of what feels natural at first
blocks.content: axis=0 does not mean summing row 0, it means summing along the row axis, which slides down through every row and leaves the columns standing. Most people get this backwards the first few times. If you are ever unsure, just check the shape of the result: summing a (2, 3) matrix along axis=0 gives shape (3,), one number per column, and along axis=1 gives shape (2,), one number per row.

blocks.text: 3.1 Min and Max Along an Axis

np.min and np.max accept the exact same axis argument, and they behave the exact same way as sum does. axis=0 gives you the minimum or maximum found in each column, and axis=1 gives you the minimum or maximum found in each row.

code.content:
print(M.min(axis=0))   # [1 2 3], smallest value in each column
print(M.max(axis=0))   # [4 5 6], largest value in each column
print(M.min(axis=1))   # [1 4], smallest value in each row
print(M.max(axis=1))   # [3 6], largest value in each row

blocks.alt: Min and Max Along an Axis
blocks.caption: Min and max are the same idea as sum, just answering a different question about the collapsed values.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972243-15843562.png

This is exactly how you would check the range of every feature column in a dataset before training a model, running min and max with axis=0 across your whole feature matrix in one line each, no loop required.
4. argmin and argmax: Finding the Position, Not the Value

np.min tells you the smallest value in an array. np.argmin tells you where that smallest value lives, the index it sits at, not the value itself. np.argmax does the same job for the largest value. This sounds like a small difference, but it turns out to be one of the most useful operations in all of applied machine learning.

code.content:
values = np.array([3, 7, 2, 9, 5])

print(np.max(values))      # 9, the value itself
print(np.argmax(values))   # 3, the index where 9 lives

print(np.min(values))      # 2, the value itself
print(np.argmin(values))   # 2, the index where 2 lives

blocks.alt: argmin and argmax: Finding the Position, Not the Value
blocks.caption: np.max hands back a value; np.argmax hands back a position. They are answering two genuinely different questions.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972244-29670984.png

blocks.title: Ties go to the first match
blocks.content: If the maximum or minimum value shows up more than once in the array, argmax and argmin always return the index of the first occurrence, reading left to right, and silently ignore every later tie. That is worth remembering if your data ever has duplicate extreme values.

blocks.text: 4.1 Predicting a Class from Classifier Scores

Here is exactly where argmax earns its keep in real ML code. A classifier does not output a class label directly, it outputs a score, or a probability, for every possible class. Turning that list of scores into an actual predicted label is a single call to argmax.

code.content:
class_names = ["cat", "dog", "rabbit"]

# one prediction for a single image: scores for cat, dog, rabbit
scores = np.array([0.10, 0.70, 0.20])
predicted_index = np.argmax(scores)
print(predicted_index)              # 1
print(class_names[predicted_index])  # dog

blocks.alt: Predicting a Class from Classifier Scores
blocks.caption: The single most common real world use of argmax: turning raw scores into the actual predicted class.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972245-343683640.png

Real models do not predict one example at a time, they predict a whole batch at once, and the scores come back as a 2-D array, one row per example, one column per class. Passing axis=1 tells argmax to find the highest scoring class within each row, giving you back one predicted class index per example in a single call.

code.content:
# a batch of 4 predictions, 3 classes each: cat, dog, rabbit
batch_scores = np.array([
    [0.10, 0.70, 0.20],
    [0.05, 0.15, 0.80],
    [0.60, 0.30, 0.10],
    [0.33, 0.34, 0.33],
])

predicted = np.argmax(batch_scores, axis=1)
print(predicted)   # [1 2 0 1]

labels = [class_names[i] for i in predicted]
print(labels)   # ['dog', 'rabbit', 'cat', 'dog']

blocks.text: That last row is a genuinely close call, 0.33, 0.34, and 0.33 are nearly tied, and argmax still commits to a single answer, index 1, since it is the largest by however small a margin. argmax never expresses uncertainty on its own, it always returns exactly one index, so if the confidence of a prediction matters to you, you need to look at the actual score values too, not just the winning index.
5. Cumulative Functions: cumsum and cumprod

Every aggregation so far has collapsed an array down to fewer numbers. Cumulative functions do something different: they keep every position in the array, but replace each one with a running result computed from everything that came before it, including itself. np.cumsum computes a running total, and np.cumprod computes a running product.

blocks.caption: Each output position is the sum of everything up to and including that point, nothing is dropped.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972246-872289963.png

Look at the shape carefully: daily_sales has shape (4,), and running_total also has shape (4,). Cumulative functions never shrink the array the way sum, min, and max do, they just replace each value with a running answer, so the output always matches the input in shape.

This running total pattern shows up constantly. A bank balance after each transaction is a cumulative sum. Total distance covered after each leg of a trip is a cumulative sum. And converting a probability density into a cumulative distribution, the probability that a value falls at or below a certain point, is also computed with exactly this same running total.

blocks.title: A quick sanity check for a proper cumulative distribution
blocks.content: If your probabilities genuinely add up to 1 across the whole array, the very last value of np.cumsum will also land on 1, since that final position is the running total of everything. If it does not, your original probabilities were not properly normalized to begin with.

blocks.text: 5.1 cumprod and a Running Product

np.cumprod is the exact same idea as cumsum, except each step multiplies instead of adds. It is the natural tool anytime a quantity compounds on itself rather than accumulating on top of itself, like year over year growth, or the combined probability of several independent events all happening in sequence.

blocks.caption: Each output position multiplies together every factor seen so far, exactly like compounding interest.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972246-318907004.png

Reading that result directly: after the first period, the value grew by 10 percent, landing at 1.10 times the original. After the second period, it grew another 20 percent on top of that, landing at 1.32 times the original. After the third period, another 5 percent brings it to 1.386 times the original. Each entry already includes every earlier multiplication, which is exactly what makes it cumulative rather than just a plain elementwise product.
6. keepdims: Keeping the Reduced Dimension Alive

By default, when np.sum, np.min, or np.max collapses a dimension, that dimension disappears from the result entirely. Passing keepdims=True changes that behavior: the dimension stays in the shape, just shrunk down to size 1 instead of being removed altogether.

code.content:
M = np.array([
    [4, 8, 6, 2],
    [1, 9, 3, 7],
    [5, 5, 5, 5],
])

row_max = M.max(axis=1)
print(row_max)          # [8 9 5]
print(row_max.shape)    # (3,) , the column dimension is gone entirely

row_max_kept = M.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print(row_max_kept)
# [[8]
#  [9]
#  [5]]
print(row_max_kept.shape)   # (3, 1) , the column dimension survives as size 1

blocks.alt: keepdims: Keeping the Reduced Dimension Alive
blocks.caption: By default, the collapsed dimension is dropped from the shape completely.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972246-191585869.png

blocks.alt: keepdims: Keeping the Reduced Dimension Alive
blocks.caption: With keepdims True, the same numbers come back, but the shape still remembers there used to be a dimension there.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972247-644171449.png

blocks.title: Same numbers, different shape
blocks.content: row_max and row_max_kept hold the exact same three numbers, 8, 9, and 5. The only difference is shape, (3,) versus (3, 1). That difference sounds cosmetic until you try to use the result together with the original array, which is exactly the next section.

blocks.text: 6.1 Broadcasting an Aggregate Back Against the Original Array

This is the entire reason keepdims exists. Once you compute an aggregate like a per row maximum, a very common next step is to use that aggregate against the original array again, for example to normalize every row by its own maximum value. That only lines up correctly if the shapes are compatible for broadcasting, and dropping the reduced dimension usually breaks that.

code.content:
M = np.array([
    [4, 8, 6, 2],
    [1, 9, 3, 7],
    [5, 5, 5, 5],
])

row_max_kept = M.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # shape (3, 1)
normalized = M / row_max_kept
print(normalized)
# [[0.5   1.    0.75  0.25 ]
#  [0.111 1.    0.333 0.778]
#  [1.    1.    1.    1.   ]]

blocks.alt: Broadcasting an Aggregate Back Against the Original Array
blocks.caption: The size 1 dimension from keepdims is exactly what lets NumPy stretch the per row max back across every column of that row.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441972720-110284512.png

Every row above now has its own maximum value scaled to exactly 1, with the rest of that row scaled proportionally. This works because a shape (3, 1) array broadcasts cleanly against a shape (3, 4) array, NumPy stretches the single column across all four columns automatically. Try the same division using row_max instead of row_max_kept, shape (3,) instead of (3, 1), and NumPy will either raise a shape error or, worse, silently broadcast against the wrong axis, since a plain (3,) shape lines up against columns by default, not rows. The full mechanics of how shapes are matched up during broadcasting get covered in the dedicated Broadcasting lesson, but keepdims is the piece that makes an aggregated result broadcastable back against its source in the first place.
7. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing axis=0 with summing row 0. axis=0 means collapsing down through every row, producing one value per column, not one value for a single row.
Reaching for np.max when you actually need the position of the maximum. If you need to know where the biggest value is, not just what it is, you want np.argmax instead.
Assuming argmax reports confidence. It only ever returns the winning index, even when the top two scores are nearly tied, so a close call and a landslide look identical from argmax alone.
Dropping keepdims and then being confused why dividing an array by its own row max throws a shape error or produces obviously wrong numbers.
Mixing up np.cumsum with np.sum. Cumsum keeps every position and returns a running total the same shape as the input; sum collapses the array down to fewer numbers entirely.

blocks.text: 8. Key Takeaway

np.sum, np.min, and np.max collapse an array down to fewer numbers, a single scalar with no axis given, or one value per row or per column once you pick an axis. np.argmin and np.argmax answer a different question entirely, handing back the index of the extreme value rather than the value itself, which is exactly how a classifier turns raw scores into a predicted label. np.cumsum and np.cumprod never shrink the array, they replace every position with a running total or running product built from everything before it.

keepdims is the small parameter with an outsized effect: it decides whether a reduced dimension vanishes or survives as size 1, and that survival is exactly what lets you broadcast an aggregated result, like a per row maximum, back against the array it came from. Mean, median, and standard deviation follow the same axis and keepdims rules as everything here, and pick up right where this lesson leaves off in the Statistical Operations lesson.
